story.title: Italy imposes €805 million fine on Meta for unauthorized photo access
story.summary: Italy's data protection authority has fined Meta €805 million for accessing the photos of approximately 20 million users without their specific consent. The fine reflects concerns over user privacy and the lack of proper notification regarding the access of their personal data.

explore_lenses.label: Why did Italy treat this as a privacy breach?
explore_lenses.title: The issue was the consent design, not just photo access
explore_lenses.summary: Italy’s regulator found that Facebook’s gallery-suggestion tool obtained a broad Android permission without clearly and separately explaining this particular use of users’ photo libraries.

claims.text: The authority said the feature was enabled by default and access was requested through one app-wide permission covering functions with different purposes; a preceding notice did not clearly disclose gallery-based post suggestions.

The regulator said Article 122 of Italy’s Privacy Code, implementing the EU ePrivacy Directive, requires free and informed consent to access information on a smartphone, regardless of whether data are transmitted or a harm is demonstrated.
Meta said the tool is a simple sharing feature, that users must grant device permission before it operates, and that they can change that permission in settings.

explore_lenses.uncertainty_note: The public regulator statement does not identify which specific photos, videos, or metadata were accessed for any individual user.

explore_lenses.label: What changes—and disputes—come next?
explore_lenses.title: Meta must redesign the feature while it challenges the ruling
explore_lenses.summary: The order requires an opt-in, clearer disclosure and default-off setting, but Meta has said it will appeal and disputes both the outcome and the proportionality of the fine.

claims.text: Within 60 days, Meta must seek separate, specific consent, clearly explain the feature and how to disable it, and keep it off by default—including for people who had previously granted gallery access.
Meta must report initial steps within 30 days and the measures it has taken within 90 days; without compliance, the feature cannot be activated for users lacking valid consent.
Meta said it would appeal, strongly disagreed with the decision, and characterized the penalty as disproportionate.
The inquiry did not examine whether gallery content was used to train AI; Meta denies such use, and the authority said it may separately assess a 2026 cloud-processing gallery feature.

story_report.summary: Italy’s data protection authority has fined Meta €805 million after finding that the company accessed the photos of about 20 million users without specific consent. The regulator said the access was tied to a feature enabled by default and to an app-wide device permission that did not clearly explain gallery-based post suggestions. Meta says users had to grant device permission and plans to appeal the penalty, which it calls disproportionate.

sections.heading: Italian regulator cites consent requirements
sections.body: The authority said Italian privacy law, implementing the EU ePrivacy Directive, requires users’ free and informed consent before information on a smartphone can be accessed. It said this requirement applies regardless of whether information is transmitted or whether harm is demonstrated. In the regulator’s account, the relevant feature relied on a single permission for functions serving different purposes, while advance notice did not clearly disclose the gallery-suggestion function.

sections.heading: Meta faces consent and reporting orders
sections.body: Within 60 days, Meta must obtain separate and specific consent, clearly explain the feature and how to turn it off, and leave it disabled by default. The order also applies to people who had previously allowed gallery access. Meta must report its initial steps within 30 days and its completed measures within 90 days; without compliance, the feature cannot be activated for users who lack valid consent.

unresolved.text: The regulator’s public statement does not specify which photos, videos or metadata were accessed for any individual user.

The inquiry did not examine whether gallery content was used to train AI. Meta denies such use, while the authority said it may separately assess a 2026 cloud-processing gallery feature; it remains unclear whether an appeal will alter the fine or compliance order.

related_stories.title: Airlines Face Major Disruptions Following Nationwide Ground Stop
related_stories.summary: Airlines in the U.S. are working to recover from a nationwide ground stop that lasted over four hours on Friday, resulting in the cancellation of more than 2,000 flights. The disruption has caused significant delays and stranded passengers, impacting travel plans across the country and internationally. Professional and college sports teams have also been affected, seeking alternative transportation options.
